results.title: Dense linear order without endpoints
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A relation $R$ on a type $\alpha$ is a *dense linear order without endpoints* if it is a strict total order (irreflexive, transitive, and trichotomous: for all $a, b$, at least one of $R(a,b)$, $a = b$, $R(b,a)$ holds), it is dense (whenever $R(a,b)$, there is $c$ with $R(a,c)$ and $R(c,b)$), and it has no endpoints (for every $a$ there are $b$ and $b'$ with $R(b,a)$ and $R(a,b')$).

results.title: Infinitely many Fibonacci pseudoprimes at twice-prime indices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F_m$ denote the $m$-th Fibonacci number. There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $n = F_{2p}$ satisfies $n > 1$, $n$ is not prime, and $n$ divides $F_{n - \left(\frac{5}{n}\right)}$, where $\left(\frac{5}{n}\right)$ is the Jacobi symbol. In other words, $F_{2p}$ is a Fibonacci pseudoprime: a composite number $n$ that divides $F_{n - \left(\frac{5}{n}\right)}$.

results.title: Pocklington's criterion for $N = Kp^e + 1$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$, $K$ and $e$ be natural numbers and let $p$ be a prime, with $0 < K < p^e$ and $N = Kp^e + 1$. If some natural number $a$ satisfies $a^{N-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{N}$ and $\gcd\big(a^{(N-1)/p} - 1, N\big) = 1$, where $(N-1)/p$ is the quotient of $N - 1$ by $p$ rounded down and $a^{(N-1)/p} - 1$ is truncated at $0$, then $N$ is prime.

results.title: Proth's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $h$ odd and $h < 2^k$, and let $N = h \cdot 2^k + 1$. Then $N$ is prime if and only if there is a residue class $a$ modulo $N$ with $a^{(N-1)/2} = -1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$.

results.title: Bonse sequence of prime indices
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $m \ge 1$ let $p_m$ be the $m$-th prime, so that $p_1 = 2$, and set $p_0 = 2$. A sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of natural numbers is a Bonse sequence if $p_{a_n}^2 < p_{a_0} p_{a_1} \cdots p_{a_{n-1}}$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

results.title: A sufficient condition for a Bonse sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers and write $A_n = a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1}$ for the product of its first $n$ terms. If there is a real number $c > 2$ such that $\log A_n / \log a_n > c$ for all sufficiently large $n$, then $a$ is a Bonse sequence.

results.title: A sufficient condition for a non-Bonse sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers and write $A_n = a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1}$ for the product of its first $n$ terms. Suppose that $(n + 1) \log \log a_n / \log a_{n+1} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, and that there is a real number $c < 2$ such that $\log A_n / \log a_n < c$ for infinitely many $n$. results.title: The $q$-weighted binary digit sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $q$ be an element of a commutative ring and let $k$ be a natural number with binary expansion $k = \sum_{i \ge 0} \omega_i 2^i$, where $\omega_i \in \{0, 1\}$. The $q$-weighted binary digit sum of $k$ is $s_q(k) = \sum_{i \ge 0} \omega_i q^{i+1}$, a finite sum because only finitely many $\omega_i$ are nonzero.

results.title: The Takagi–Landsberg function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real or complex parameter $a$ and a real number $x$, let $\tau(y)$ denote the distance from a real number $y$ to the nearest integer. The Takagi–Landsberg function is $\mathcal{T}_a(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a^n \tau(2^n x)$, where the value is taken to be $0$ when the series does not converge absolutely. The series converges for $|a| < 1$, and at dyadic rationals $x$ it is a finite sum.

results.title: Substitutions in the sense of Labbé and Lepšová
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A substitution is a map $\eta$ sending each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, such that $\eta$ is non-erasing (the word $\eta(a)$ is nonempty for every letter $a \in A$) and some letter $a \in A$ is growing, that is, $|\eta^k(a)| \to \infty$ as $k \to \infty$, where $\eta^k$ is the $k$-th iterate of $\eta$. The alphabet $A$ need not be finite.

results.title: Substitutions are non-erasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every substitution $\eta$ in the sense of Labbé and Lepšová is non-erasing: $\eta(a)$ is a nonempty word for every letter $a$.

results.title: Admissible sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\eta$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, and let $k \ge 0$. A finite sequence $(m_i, a_i)_{0 \le i \le k}$ of pairs, each made of a finite word $m_i$ over $A$ and a letter $a_i \in A$, is admissible with respect to $\eta$ when the word $m_i a_i$ is a prefix of $\eta(a_{i+1})$ for every $i < k$.

results.title: Admissible sequences starting from a letter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\eta$ map each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$, and let $a \in A$. A finite sequence $(m_i, a_i)_{0 \le i \le k}$ of pairs, each made of a finite word $m_i$ over $A$ and a letter $a_i \in A$, is $a$-admissible when it is admissible with respect to $\eta$ and moreover the word $m_k a_k$ is a prefix of $\eta(a)$.

results.title: One-term sequences are admissible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\eta$ send each letter of an alphabet $A$ to a finite word over $A$. Every one-term sequence $(m_0, a_0)$, with $m_0$ a finite word over $A$ and $a_0 \in A$, is admissible with respect to $\eta$: the admissibility condition is vacuous for a sequence with the single index $0$.

results.title: The substitution automaton on the empty word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every letter map $\eta$ and every letter $b$, the substitution automaton $\mathcal{A}_{\eta,\cdot}$ started at $b$ ends in the state $b$ after reading the empty digit word.

results.title: Reading a nonempty digit word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\eta$ be a letter map, $b$ a letter, $i$ a digit and $w$ a digit word. If $i < |\eta(b)|$, then the value of the substitution automaton started at $b$ on the word $iw$ (the digit $i$ followed by $w$) equals its value started at $\eta(b)_i$ on $w$, where $\eta(b)_i$ is the letter of $\eta(b)$ at position $i$, counting from $0$. If $i \ge |\eta(b)|$, the run on $iw$ is undefined.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\eta$ be a substitution on an alphabet $A$, extended to finite words by concatenation, and let $(m_i, a_i)_{0 \le i \le k}$ be a sequence of pairs of a finite word $m_i$ over $A$ and a letter $a_i \in A$ that is admissible with respect to $\eta$. Then $\sum_{j=0}^{k} |\eta^j(m_j)| < |\eta^k(m_k a_k)|$, where $\eta^j$ is the $j$-th iterate of $\eta$ and $|w|$ is the length of a word $w$.

results.title: Path tree on a vertex list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a vertex $r$ and a list of vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the spine is the rooted tree $r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$: its root is $r$, each vertex has the next one in the list as its only child, and the last vertex ($c_k$, or $r$ when $k = 0$) is a leaf.

results.title: Forest from a vertex list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The forest built from the empty list is empty; the forest built from a list $r, c_1, \dots, c_k$ consists of the single spine $r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$, the rooted tree in which each vertex has the next one as its only child.

results.title: Tree of a forest containing a vertex
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Removing the trees that contain a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a vertex $x$ and a forest, given as a list of rooted ordered trees, removing the trees containing $x$ deletes from the list every tree that has $x$ among its vertices and keeps the remaining trees in their original order.

results.title: Removing the tree containing a vertex splits the forest's vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a forest of rooted ordered trees whose concatenated vertex lists have no duplicates, let $x$ be a vertex, and let $t$ be the first tree of $f$ containing $x$. Then the concatenated vertex list of the forest obtained from $f$ by removing every tree containing $x$, followed by the vertex list of $t$, is a permutation of the concatenated vertex list of $f$.

results.title: Subtree rooted at a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a tree $T$, the subtree of $T$ rooted at the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder, or nothing when $x$ does not occur in $T$.

results.title: Adjacency in a rooted tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a rooted tree $t$ when they are joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in either direction: some node of $t$ labelled $a$ has a child labelled $b$, or some node of $t$ labelled $b$ has a child labelled $a$.

results.title: The first endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $a$ is a vertex of $t$.

results.title: Adjacency in a tree is symmetric
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and vertices $a$ and $b$, if $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $T$ (joined by a parent-child edge in either direction), then $b$ and $a$ are adjacent in $T$.

results.title: The second endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $b$ is a vertex of $t$.

results.title: Adjacency test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For vertices $a$, $b$ and a rooted tree $t$ with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the adjacency test of $a$ and $b$ in $t$ returns true exactly when $r = a$ and some $c_i$ has root $b$, or $r = b$ and some $c_i$ has root $a$, or the adjacency test of $a$ and $b$ returns true in some $c_i$.

results.title: Grafting a tree below a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a vertex $y$ and trees $N$ and $T$, grafting $N$ at $y$ in $T$ attaches $N$ as a new last child of the first node of $T$ labelled $y$ in preorder, keeping every existing node and edge; it returns nothing when $y$ does not occur in $T$. This is the tree surgery behind linking two trees: it adds exactly the edge from $y$ to the root of $N$.

results.title: Vertices after grafting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ and $C$ be trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $C$ at $y$ in $t$, that is, attaching $C$ as a new last child of a node labelled $y$, produces the tree $t'$, then for every $v$, $v$ is a vertex of $t'$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of $t$ or a vertex of $C$.

results.title: Grafting keeps the root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ and $N$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $N$ into $T$ at $y$ is defined and yields the tree $T'$, then the root of $T'$ equals the root of $T$.

results.title: Edges after grafting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ and $u$ be rooted trees and $y$ a vertex, and suppose that grafting $u$ as a new child under $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$. Then for all vertices $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are adjacent in $t$, or adjacent in $u$, or $a = y$ and $b$ is the root of $u$, or $a$ is the root of $u$ and $b = y$.

results.title: Grafting adds the new subtree's vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ and $s$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $s$ as a new child at $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$, then the vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t$ followed by the vertex list of $s$.

results.title: Rerooting a tree at a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$ with root $r$, rerooting $T$ at $x$ is defined recursively. If $r = x$, the result is $T$ itself. Otherwise let $C$ be the first child subtree of $r$ that contains $x$, let $p$ be the root of $C$, and let $C'$ be $C$ rerooted at $x$. The result is $C'$ with the tree formed by $r$ and its remaining children (in their original order) attached as a new last child of the…

results.title: Rerooting fails at an absent vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and every vertex $x$ that is not a vertex of $T$, rerooting $T$ at $x$ is undefined (it returns no tree).

results.title: Rerooting preserves the vertex set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then a vertex lies in $t'$ if and only if it lies in $t$.

results.title: Rerooting keeps every edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex, and suppose that rerooting $t$ at a vertex $x$ yields the tree $t'$. Then for all vertices $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are adjacent in $t$.

results.title: Rerooting preserves the vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then the vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t$.

results.title: Pruning the subtrees rooted at a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$, pruning $T$ at $x$ removes every subtree of $T$ whose root is labelled $x$, keeping every other node and edge and the order of children. If the root of $T$ is $x$, nothing remains and pruning is undefined. Otherwise the result is the tree with the same root whose children are, in their original order, the pruned children of the root, with the children labelled $x$…

results.title: Pruning at an absent vertex changes nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex that does not occur in $t$. Then pruning the subtrees rooted at $x$ from $t$ succeeds and returns $t$ itself.

results.title: Vertices of a pruned tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning $t$ at $x$ leaves the tree $t'$, then every vertex of $t'$ is a vertex of $t$ and is different from $x$.

results.title: Pruning keeps the vertices outside the detached subtree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree whose preorder vertex list has no repeated vertex, and let $x$ be a vertex. Suppose the subtree search finds the subtree $s$ of $t$ rooted at $x$, and pruning $t$ at $x$ leaves the tree $t'$. Then every vertex of $t$ that is not a vertex of $s$ is a vertex of $t'$.

results.title: Pruning a subtree splits the vertex list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree whose vertex list has no duplicates and let $x$ be a vertex. If $x$ occurs in $t$, with $s$ the subtree of $t$ rooted at $x$, and pruning at $x$ leaves a tree $t'$ (that is, $x$ is not the root of $t$), then the vertex list of $t$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t'$ followed by the vertex list of $s$.

results.title: Pruning keeps the root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning $T$ at $x$ yields a tree $T'$ (that is, the root of $T$ is not $x$), then the root of $T'$ equals the root of $T$.

results.title: Pruning keeps surviving edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex and $x$ a vertex, and suppose that removing every subtree rooted at $x$ from $t$ leaves the tree $t'$ (that is, the root of $t$ is not $x$). If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$ and both are vertices of $t'$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$.

results.title: Root-to-vertex path
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$, the root path of $x$ is defined exactly when $x$ is a vertex of $T$. It is then the list of vertices on the path from the root of $T$ down to $x$, root first and ending with $x$; if $x$ occurs more than once, the path leads to its first occurrence in preorder.

results.title: A root path ends at its target
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $p$ is the path from the root of a tree $T$ down to a vertex $x$ of $T$, then $p$ is nonempty and its last (deepest) vertex is $x$.

results.title: The root path starts at the root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ (the path from the root of $t$ down to $x$) is defined and equals $p$, then $p$ is nonempty and its first vertex is the root of $t$.

results.title: Root paths stay inside the tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $p$ is the path in a tree $t$ from the root down to a vertex $x$, then every vertex of $p$ is a vertex of $t$.

results.title: Root paths have distinct vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the preorder vertex list of a rooted tree $t$ has no repeated vertex and $p$ is the path from the root of $t$ down to a vertex $x$, then $p$ has no repeated vertex.

results.title: Consecutive vertices of a root path are adjacent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every $i < k$ the vertices $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in one direction or the other.

results.title: Parent-child relation in a rooted tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For vertices $a$ and $b$ and a rooted ordered tree $t$, $a$ is a parent of $b$ in $t$ when some node of $t$ labelled $a$ has a child subtree whose root is $b$. Preferred edges of a link-cut tree are directed this way, from a node to its preferred child.

results.title: Parent-child edges are edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every rooted tree $t$ and all vertices $a$ and $b$, if $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in $t$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$.

results.title: The parent endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in a tree $t$, then $a$ is a vertex of $t$.

results.title: The child endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in a tree $t$, then $b$ is a vertex of $t$.

results.title: A root path follows parent-child edges downward
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every $i < k$ the vertex $p_i$ is the parent of $p_{i+1}$ somewhere in $t$.

results.title: Consecutive edges of a vertex path
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$, its path edges are the ordered pairs $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{n-1}, v_n)$ of consecutive vertices, in this order; a list with at most one vertex has no path edges. For a path listed from the root downward each pair is (parent, child), and the preferred edges installed by an access to a vertex $x$ are the path edges of the root-to-$x$ path.

results.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $E$ of preferred edges, each a pair (parent, preferred child), the decomposition of a tree $T$ is a pair (down, rest): down is the preferred path that starts at the root of $T$ and follows edges of $E$ downward, and rest is the list of all other preferred paths of $T$. When a node has several children joined to it by edges of $E$ (excluded in valid states, where each vertex has at most one preferred…

results.title: Preferred paths of a tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and let $E$ be a list of preferred edges, each a pair (parent, child). The preferred paths of $t$ under $E$ are listed as follows: first the downward path of the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$, which starts at the root of $t$ and follows preferred edges downward, and then all other paths of that decomposition, in the order the decomposition returns them.

results.title: The downward preferred path starts at the root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of preferred edges, the downward preferred path in the preferred-path decomposition of a tree is nonempty and its first vertex is the root of the tree.

results.title: Preferred paths permute the vertex list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of preferred edges, the downward preferred path of a tree followed by the concatenation of the other paths of its preferred-path decomposition is a permutation of the vertex list of the tree.

results.title: The preferred paths of a tree rearrange its vertex list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $E$ of directed edges and every rooted ordered tree $t$, the concatenation of the preferred paths of $t$ under $E$ is a permutation of the preorder vertex list of $t$.

results.title: Decomposition paths are paths of the tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of preferred edges, in the preferred-path decomposition of a tree $T$, the downward preferred path and every other path are paths of $T$: any two consecutive vertices are joined by a parent-child edge of $T$, in either direction.

results.title: Preferred paths of a tree follow tree edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a tree and $E$ any list of pairs of vertices, read as preferred (parent, child) edges. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$ and every $i < k$, the vertices $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in one direction or the other.

results.title: Access edges make the root path the downward preferred path
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a tree whose vertex list is duplicate-free, let $x$ be a vertex of $T$ with root path $p$ (the path from the root of $T$ down to $x$), and let $E$ be a list of directed edges such that every consecutive pair of $p$, parent first, lies in $E$, and every edge of $E$ whose first vertex lies on $p$ is such a consecutive pair. Then the downward preferred path of the preferred-path decomposition of $T$ under…

results.title: Link-cut tree state
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A state of a link-cut tree over a vertex type $V$ consists of the represented forest, a list of rooted ordered trees with vertices in $V$, and a list of preferred (solid) edges, each a pair $(u, v)$ of vertices meant as the edge from a node $u$ to its preferred child $v$ in the represented forest; the structure itself does not require these pairs to be edges of the forest. The preferred-path decomposition is…

results.title: Vertex of a link-cut tree state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A vertex $x$ belongs to a link-cut tree state $s$ when $x$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$.

results.title: Connectivity in a link-cut tree state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected in a link-cut tree state $s$ when some tree of the represented forest of $s$ has both $x$ and $y$ among its vertices.

results.title: Connectivity via Euler tours
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a link-cut tree state $s$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, $x$ and $y$ are connected in $s$ if and only if some tree of the represented forest of $s$ contains both $x$ and $y$ in its Euler tour.

results.title: Valid link-cut tree states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A link-cut tree state $s$ is valid when four conditions hold: the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of its represented forest has no duplicates (so the trees are vertex-disjoint); its list of preferred edges has no duplicates; every preferred edge $(a, b)$ is a parent-child edge of some tree of the represented forest, with $a$ the parent of $b$; and any two preferred edges with the same parent are…

results.title: Validity of states with no preferred edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state whose list of preferred edges is empty. If the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of the represented forest of $s$ has no duplicates, then $s$ is valid.

results.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a link-cut tree state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a link-cut tree state $s$, its preferred paths are obtained by taking, for each represented tree of $s$ in forest order, the preferred paths of that tree under the preferred edges of $s$, and concatenating these lists. Within a tree these are its maximal chains of preferred edges when each vertex has at most one preferred child, each listed from its shallowest to its deepest vertex; a vertex incident to no…

results.title: Preferred paths cover exactly the vertices of the forest
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $v$, $v$ lies on some path of the preferred-path decomposition of $s$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$. No validity hypothesis on $s$ is needed.

results.title: Preferred paths cover each vertex at most once
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a valid link-cut tree state, the concatenation of all preferred paths of the decomposition has no repeated vertex: no vertex occurs twice on one path or on two different paths.

results.title: Preferred paths are pairwise vertex-disjoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a valid link-cut tree state, any two preferred paths at different positions of the preferred-path decomposition have no vertex in common.

results.title: Preferred paths have distinct vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every preferred path of a valid state has distinct vertices.

results.title: Preferred paths of a link-cut tree state follow represented edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in the preferred-path decomposition of $s$ and every $i < k$, some represented tree of $s$ has $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ adjacent, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in one direction or the other.

results.title: Access in a link-cut tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex. If $x$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$, let $T$ be the first such tree and let $p$ be the path in $T$ from its root down to $x$. Accessing $x$ keeps the represented forest and replaces the preferred edges by those preferred edges of $s$ whose parent endpoint is not on $p$, followed by the edges of $p$, each directed from parent to child.…

results.title: Access keeps off-path preferred edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, $x$ a vertex, and $(u, w)$ a preferred edge of $s$, directed from the parent $u$ to the child $w$. Suppose that, if some tree of the represented forest of $s$ contains $x$, then $u$ does not lie on the path in the first such tree from its root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then $(u, w)$ is still a preferred edge after accessing $x$.

results.title: Access makes the root path preferred
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex, let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains $x$, and let $p$ be the path in $t$ from the root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then every edge of $p$, taken as the pair (parent, child) of consecutive vertices of $p$, is a preferred edge of the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$.

results.title: Access leaves the represented forest unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $x$, accessing $x$ changes only the preferred edges: the represented forest of the resulting state equals the represented forest of $s$.

results.title: After access, the accessed vertex ends its preferred path
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ be a vertex of its represented forest. Then, after accessing $x$, the preferred-path decomposition of the new state contains a path $p$ whose last vertex is $x$, and $p$ is the path from the root down to $x$ in some tree of the represented forest of $s$.

results.title: Access preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a link-cut tree state $s$ is valid, then for every vertex $x$ the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$ is again valid.

results.title: Making a vertex the root in a link-cut tree state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a vertex $x$ and a state $s$, the state $\operatorname{makeRoot}(x, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its forest is defined as follows. If $x$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise the first represented tree containing $x$ is rerooted at $x$: the edges on the path from its old root to $x$ are reversed, and when the tree has distinct vertices every undirected edge…

results.title: Making a vertex the root installs a tree rooted there
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex of its represented forest. After making $x$ the root, some represented tree has root $x$ and contains $x$ as a vertex.

results.title: Making a vertex the root keeps its connections
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be connected in $s$. Then $x$ and $y$ are still connected in the state obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented tree.

results.title: Rerooting a link-cut tree state preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every valid link-cut tree state $s$ and every vertex $x$, the state obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented tree is valid.

results.title: Linking two trees of a link-cut tree state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given vertices $x$ and $y$ and a state $s$, the state $\operatorname{link}(x, y, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its forest is defined as follows. If $x$ or $y$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise let $t_x$ and $t_y$ be the first represented trees containing $x$ and $y$. results.title: Linking connects the endpoints
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be vertices of its represented forest. Then in the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ to $y$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected, that is, some represented tree contains both. No invariant on the state is needed.

results.title: Linking in a link-cut tree preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every valid link-cut tree state $s$ and all vertices $x$ and $y$, the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ and $y$ is valid.

results.title: Cutting off the subtree at a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Cutting at a vertex $x$ resets the preferred edges of the state to the empty list and changes its forest as follows. If no tree of the forest contains $x$, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise let $T$ be the first tree containing $x$ and $S$ the first subtree of $T$ rooted at $x$ in preorder. Every tree containing $x$ is removed from the forest, and two trees are appended at the end: first the remainder of $T$ with…

results.title: A cut disconnects a vertex from everything outside its subtree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, let $t$ be the first tree of its represented forest containing the vertex $x$, and let $u$ be the first subtree of $t$ in preorder whose root is $x$. After cutting $s$ at $x$, the vertex $x$ is not connected to any vertex $y$ that is not a vertex of $u$.

results.title: Both sides of a cut remain in the forest
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, let $x$ and $y$ be vertices, and let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains $x$. Suppose no vertex occurs twice in $t$, and let $T_x$ be the subtree of $t$ rooted at $x$. If $y$ is a vertex of $t$ but not of $T_x$, then after cutting $s$ at $x$ both $x$ and $y$ are vertices of the represented forest.

results.title: Cutting preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for every vertex $x$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting off the subtree rooted at $x$ is again valid.

results.title: Cutting an edge of a link-cut tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For vertices $x$ and $y$ and a link-cut tree state $s$, cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ works as follows. If $x$ and $y$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$, the result is obtained from $s$ by first making $x$ the root of its represented tree and then cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$. Otherwise the represented forest is left unchanged. In both cases the list of preferred edges…

results.title: Edge cut on an adjacent pair
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ in $s$ gives the same state as first making $x$ the root of its represented tree and then cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$.

results.title: Edge cut on a non-adjacent pair
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in no tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ in $s$ leaves the represented forest unchanged and makes the list of preferred edges empty.

results.title: Edge cutting preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for all vertices $x$ and $y$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ is again valid.

results.title: Cutting an edge separates its endpoints
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. After the edge cut of $x$ and $y$ in $s$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are not connected: no represented tree contains both.

results.title: An edge cut keeps every other edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of its represented forest. If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$, and neither $a = x$ and $b = y$ nor $a = y$ and $b = x$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest obtained from $s$ by cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$.

results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For an answer type $R$ and a simple type $A$, the type of call-by-name computations of type $A$ is $C(A) = (A^\ast \to R) \to R$, where $A^\ast$ is the call-by-name CPS translation of $A$.

results.caption: Definition

results.summary: A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ consists of a relation $<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). results.title: Strict total order from a relation (Arrow's theorem)
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A relation $<$ on a type $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on $\alpha$.

results.title: Preference relation of a strict total order (Arrow's theorem)
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a strict total order $T$ on a type $\alpha$, this is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$.

results.title: Irreflexivity of strict preference (Arrow's theorem)
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $T$ be a strict total order on a type $\alpha$, and write $a \lt _T b$ for its relation. Then for every $a \in \alpha$, $a \lt _T a$ does not hold.

results.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem are transitive
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: If $<$ is a strict total order on a type $\alpha$ and $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.

results.title: Strict preference orders for Arrow's theorem are total
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: If $<$ is a strict total order on a type $\alpha$ and $a, b \in \alpha$ are distinct, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.

results.title: Preference profile (Arrow's theorem)
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A profile assigns to each voter a strict total order on the alternatives.

results.title: Social welfare function
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A social welfare function maps each unrestricted profile to a social strict total order.

results.title: Pareto condition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A social welfare function $F$ satisfies the Pareto condition if for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever every voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.

results.title: Independence of irrelevant alternatives
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A social welfare function $F$ satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives if for all profiles $p_1, p_2$ and all alternatives $a, b$ the following holds: if every voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p_1$ exactly when that voter strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p_2$, then $F(p_1)$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ exactly when $F(p_2)$ does.

results.title: Dictator of a social welfare function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A voter $d$ is a dictator for a social welfare function $F$ if for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever $d$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.

results.title: Dictatorial social welfare function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A social welfare function $F$ is dictatorial if some voter $d$ is a dictator for $F$: for every profile $p$ and all alternatives $a, b$, whenever $d$ strictly prefers $a$ to $b$ in $p$, the social order $F(p)$ also strictly prefers $a$ to $b$.

results.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem for strict preferences, general form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Suppose there are finitely many alternatives, at least three of them, and finitely many voters, at least one. Then every social welfare function, which assigns a strict total order of the alternatives to each profile of strict total orders (one per voter), that satisfies the Pareto condition and independence of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial.

Then every social welfare function, which assigns a strict total order of the alternatives to each profile of strict total orders (one per voter), that satisfies the Pareto condition and independence of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial.
